conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past week.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team that supports you; there’s no judgment here—just a safe space to talk honestly. The whole thing takes only a few minutes, and your answers help us figure out the best next steps for your care. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.  

**Question 1:** Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that usually lift your mood, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? I still enjoy some things—like when my baby smiles or when I get ten quiet minutes with a cup of tea—but it feels dimmer. Stuff that used to feel exciting, like texting a friend or watching a favorite show, just lands flat most days.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh—especially when my husband makes a silly face at the baby—but it takes more effort than it used to. It feels like I have to remind myself to find things funny instead of just naturally cracking up the way I did before she was born.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I’ll plan a coffee date or a walk with the stroller, and part of me hopes it’ll feel fun, but mostly I’m just thinking about everything that could go wrong—her getting fussy, me spilling on myself, how tired I’ll be after. The excitement I used to feel ahead of stuff just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… like if she won’t settle at night, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding her right or I missed her sleepy cues.” I know rationally babies just cry, but I still catch myself thinking it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

That happens a few times a week. Out of nowhere my chest feels tight and I start thinking, “What if she stops breathing in her sleep?” or “What if I drop her?” Nothing’s actually wrong in that moment, but the worry just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a couple of times. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I have to put the baby in the crib for a minute so I can sit down and breathe. There’s no real danger; it just hits out of nowhere and then fades after ten or fifteen minutes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I manage, but by late afternoon it feels like the laundry, dishes, and her next feed all pile up at once. Some evenings I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking, “I can’t keep up,” and feel this heavy tiredness that makes even folding a onesie feel like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy-more just keyed-up. When I finally lie down, my mind replays every little thing I did that day-did I burp her long enough, was that rash normal-and I can't settle. Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, then I'm up again when she cries. It's more the busy thoughts than feeling miserable that keeps me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some days—like yesterday I just sat in the rocker with her and teared up for no clear reason. It’s not every day, and it’s not all day long, but the sadness sneaks in and hangs around for an hour or two before it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve felt teary a couple of mornings when exhaustion hits, but I haven’t actually cried—no full-on sobs or anything—since the baby came home.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I’ve never had any thoughts like that, and I wouldn’t want to leave my baby or my family.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit

Symptoms endorsed
- Markedly reduced enjoyment/anticipation (Q2)
- Daily heightened anxiety and episodic panic without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)
- Frequent self-blame/guilt regarding infant care (Q3)
- Intermittent sadness or tearfulness, not pervasive but noticeable (Q8)
- Sleep-onset difficulty driven by intrusive worries rather than infant demands alone (Q7)
- Afternoon sense of being overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)

Pattern
Mood and anxiety symptoms cluster in late afternoon/evening; still able to experience pleasure with effort; no anhedonia or motor slowing; no self-harm ideation (Q10).

Areas of screening significance
- Possible adjustment-level depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety features
- No current safety concerns

Risk factors present
Loss of pleasure, excessive guilt, anxiety/panic episodes, sleep disruption linked to rumination, perceived inability to manage daily tasks; absence of suicidal thinking.

Summary
Patient reports sub-threshold but distressing mood and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery; symptoms interfere with sleep and daily functioning yet preserve capacity for positive affect and no self-harm risk. Screen suggests monitoring for worsening mood or anxiety; consider standardized postpartum depression/anxiety scale and follow-up within 1–2 weeks.
